Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

72.8% of Illinois's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 72.8% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 20.7% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Flood insurance cost in Illinois

In Illinois, typically about $1,136 a year ($95 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $773 and $1,515. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $773 · Typical $1,136 · A quarter pay over $1,515 · A tenth pay $2,262 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 17,352 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay.

Source: floodsmart.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Wait exceptions, exclusions, premium increases and surcharges, aid, appeals, rebuilding and closing rules: the NFIP rules in full.

Your state's insurance regulator: Illinois Department of Insurance.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Illinois: what floods pay out

Floods in Illinois have led to 51,256 NFIP flood claims and $579.7 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2008, 2013 and 1993.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2008 ($104,835,282), 2013 ($93,078,418), 1993 ($67,286,121). Total paid $579,666,156. Totals for 2025 and 2026 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 80.4% of claims in Illinois paid something. The average paid claim was $14,444 (all years, in dollars of the day, not adjusted for inflation).

Typical claim: the median paid building claim was $5,035.

  • Average paid claim, incl. code-upgrade (ICC) pay$14,444
  • No recorded payment19.6%
  • Claims that paid41,188

FEMA's claim records give a reason when a building claim has no recorded payment, such as damage less than the deductible, not an actual flood, seepage or backed-up drains. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years. All years, records FEMA coded as entered in error left out (the claims page uses losses from 2020 on, so its shares differ). FEMA's data has no open or closed field, so a recent claim with no payment may still be paid.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 32.5% of the 11,239 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 11,239 policies reporting one)32.5%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)45.3%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 39,061 claims paid with a damage figure)6.9%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 13, 2026.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $939 a year (Zone X) to $1,293 (Zone AE) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

Flood zoneMedian / yrPriced policies

Zone X$9395,426
Zone A$9571,263
Zone AH$1,211779
Zone C$1,186296
Zone A13$1,174125

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

Source: ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Why do sites quote different prices for Illinois?

Because they measure different things. Existing single-family policies here typically cost $1,136 a year, and policies first bought in the past year $1,095; other sites count other policies, years or averages.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Typical cost, single-family homes (median)$1,136premium plus fees; the middle policy
Typical premium only$902before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Typical cost, policies whose term began Jan–Aug 2026$1,16811,620 policies
Typical cost, policies first bought in the past year$1,0951,492 policies, past year
FEMA's full-risk premium (median)$1,024the price FEMA's model sets for these existing policies
Full-risk premium plus average fees$1,284what these existing policies would cost at FEMA's full price
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$1,306pulled up by a few expensive policies
Average cost, every policy type$1,696adds condos, rentals and businesses

Condo owners: condo-unit policies are 1.9% of NFIP policy units here and whole condo buildings 0.9%. The every-policy-type average includes them. Condo-unit policies here have a median cost of $581 a year (premium plus fees, 593 priced policies; condo flood insurance by state). The single-family figures leave out every policy FEMA marks as a condo unit or a whole condo building.

All from the NFIP policies in force on August 31, 2026. How this is counted

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

33.8% of single-family primary-home policies in Illinois have a premium below FEMA's full-risk premium, so those policies' bills are rising toward it. Median premium $902, full-risk $1,024 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$902
  • Median full-risk premium$1,024
  • Pay below full-risk33.8% of 17,352

Yearly cap: By law, most premium rates may not rise more than 18% a year (42 U.S.C. §4015(e)).

Source: agents.floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How Illinois appears in the national research papers

Each paper measures one thing in FEMA's records for every U.S. county with enough records. A fifth is a position in a list, not a grade or a prediction.

  • Outside the zone: paid flood claims rated outside high-risk zones: 9 of this state's counties have at least 100 claims with a payment and a rated zone and are listed.

Can I pay less?

The usual building deductible here is $2,000 (39.1% of single-family policies). FEMA's ways that may lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 190,529 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once; 33,098 records are from homes FEMA's disaster-aid data flags as severe repeat-loss (SRL).

  • Repeat-flood damage records190,529
  • Records from homes flagged severe repeat-loss (SRL)33,098

These count damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Individual Assistance Multiple-Loss Flood Properties. Data: FEMA's current multiple-loss list; retrieved November 13, 2026.

How often is Illinois a flood disaster?

41 federal disasters for floods or storms here; the latest was Severe Storms, Tornadoes, Straight-Line Winds, and Floodng (2024).

  • September 2024 — Severe Storms, Tornadoes, Straight-Line Winds, and Floodng
  • November 2023 — Severe Storms and Flooding
  • August 2023 — Severe Storms and Flooding
  • October 2022 — Severe Storm and Flooding
  • September 2019 — Severe Storms and Flooding
  • May 2013 — Severe Storms, Straight-Line Winds, and Flooding

Only the latest are listed, newest first; disasters with the same month and title share one line, which says how many; the count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Disaster Declarations Summaries. Data: declarations through 2024; retrieved November 13, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $973.6 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $2,932 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 13, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted.

In-force count: 30,756 policy units (from 23,806 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit).
